exercises.approach: Define `median <- function(x, ...) -999` in the global environment, then call both `median(c(1, 4, 9))` and `stats::median(c(1, 4, 9))`.
exercises.why: An unqualified name is looked up from the global environment outward, so the mask is found first. `stats::` goes straight to the stats exports, which return the middle value, 4.
exercises.wrong: Assuming the package function wins because stats is attached. A script run in a session where someone defined median gets -999 and no warning.

exercises.why: The lookup goes through the stats export list, not the search path, so the global mask is never consulted and the median of 1, 4 and 9 is 4.
exercises.wrong: Using `get("median")`. It searches from the calling environment and returns the -999 mask; calling library(stats) does not help, since the global environment is still searched first.

exercises.approach: Create the tree under `tempfile()` with `on.exit(unlink(root, recursive = TRUE))`, write the three files, read them back with read.dcf, readLines and parse, then `sys.source()` the R file into an environment whose parent is baseenv().
exercises.why: parse confirms two top-level definitions before anything runs, and the fresh environment holds only those definitions, so the mean of 2 and 4, which is 3, comes from the authored code alone.
exercises.wrong: Running `source()` into the global environment. The definitions would overwrite the session's observed_mean, and a stray global helper could satisfy a missing reference and hide the bug.

exercises.approach: Read NAMESPACE to decide what is public: it lists only `export(observed_mean)`, so .validate is internal because it is not exported.
exercises.why: A leading dot only hides a name from a default ls() listing; it has no effect on exports. A NAMESPACE using `exportPattern(".")` would export .validate despite the dot.
exercises.wrong: Treating the dot as the access rule. Under a broad export pattern, the helper becomes part of the public interface while its author still thinks it is private.
exercises.verify: `readLines(file.path(root, "NAMESPACE"))` returns only "export(observed_mean)", and `ls(environment)` omits .validate while `ls(environment, all.names = TRUE)` shows it.

exercises.approach: Test `observed_mean(numeric(0))` and `observed_mean(c(1, Inf))` as two separate cases with different expected outcomes.
exercises.why: An empty vector passes the finite check, because any() of nothing is FALSE, and the length guard returns NA_real_. Inf fails is.finite, so the function stops before averaging.
exercises.wrong: Dropping the length guard and relying on mean. The empty case would return NaN, which differs from the documented NA_real_, and filtering out Inf would silently average 1 alone.
exercises.verify: `is.na(observed_mean(numeric(0)))` returns TRUE, and `observed_mean(c(1, Inf))` stops with "finite numeric values required".

exercises.approach: List the remaining steps for a separate project: document, build, install into a library, run R CMD check with tests, and confirm that Imports: stats resolves when the namespace loads.
exercises.why: parse and sys.source only evaluated one file. No namespace was created, so the export list was never applied and the DESCRIPTION fields were never checked by R.
exercises.wrong: Claiming a working package because observed_mean returned 3. That proves one function evaluates, not that the package installs or checks; network installation also does not belong in this pad.
exercises.verify: `exists(".validate", envir = environment)` returns TRUE in the sys.source environment, which shows that the export list was not enforced.

run_note: The starter supplies the values 1, 4 and 9 and the package name measurekit. Run it, then define a global function named `median` that returns -999 and compare it with `stats::median()`, which still returns 4. Build the DESCRIPTION, NAMESPACE and R source files under a `tempfile()` directory only, never in your project tree.
checks_note: The assertions confirm that DESCRIPTION names measurekit, that NAMESPACE contains exactly `export(observed_mean)`, that the source parses into two expressions and computes a mean of 3, that a masking global median returns -999 while `stats::median()` returns 4, that an empty input returns NA, and that `dnorm(0)` matches its closed form. They do not install or check the package; parsing a tree is not `R CMD check`.
